slides.title: faculty of arts
slides.summary: This lecture introduces the third session on language models and word meaning within the Faculty of Arts' Computational Linguistics course. The session is led by Professor Tim Van de Cruys and took place on Tuesday, October 6, 2026.

slides.title: Tokenization
slides.summary: Computers encode text as a sequence of characters where words, spaces, and punctuation are treated identically. Because this uniform encoding obscures linguistic structure, tokenization is required to explicitly define and mark word boundaries within the string.

slides.title: Tokenization
slides.summary: Tokenization addresses the fundamental question of defining a word as a consecutive sequence of characters separated by whitespace or punctuation. The slide highlights the specific challenge posed by apostrophes, illustrating how they complicate this definition in cases like "sms'en," "gsm'etje," and "doin'."

slides.title: Tokenization
slides.summary: Tokenization addresses the fundamental question of defining a word as a consecutive sequence of characters separated by whitespace or punctuation. The slide highlights specific ambiguities in this definition, particularly regarding how to handle apostrophes (e.g., "sms'en", "doin'") and hyphens (e.g., "self-driving", "what-do-you-mean-look"). These examples illustrate the complexity of determining whether such characters act as separators or integral parts of a single token.

slides.title: Tokenization
slides.summary: Tokenization involves defining a word as a consecutive sequence of characters separated by whitespace or punctuation, though this definition faces challenges with apostrophes (e.g., "doin'") and hyphens (e.g., "self-driving"). Complications arise in languages lacking separation markers, such as compound words in Dutch ("langeafstandsloper"), Chinese scripts without whitespace, and agglutinating languages like Turkish, Basque, and Inuit.

slides.title: Tokenization
slides.summary: Tokenization involves determining what constitutes a "word" within a text. A key challenge arises with proper names, such as "San Francisco" and "New York," which consist of multiple tokens but represent single entities. This slide highlights the ambiguity in defining word boundaries when processing multi-word geographical names.

slides.title: Tokenization
slides.summary: Tokenization addresses the fundamental challenge of defining what constitutes a "word" in computational linguistics. The slide highlights that this definition is complicated by proper names like "San Francisco" and fixed expressions such as "by and large," "piece of cake," and "spill the beans". These examples illustrate cases where standard word boundaries may not align with semantic units, requiring specific handling during the tokenization process.

slides.title: Tokenization
slides.summary: Tokenization addresses the challenge of defining a "word," particularly for proper names like "San Francisco" and fixed expressions such as "by and large". Modern neural models circumvent this ambiguity by splitting text into frequency-based subword units, which can be smaller than whole words. A primary example of this approach is byte pair encoding, a topic that will be explored further later in the course.

slides.title: Sentence detection
slides.summary: Sentence detection relies on punctuation, where characters like '?' and '!' are unambiguous markers of sentence boundaries. However, the dot ('.') is highly ambiguous because it appears in abbreviations such as "U.N." or "etc." within sentences. Consequently, context is essential to accurately determine whether a dot signifies the end of a sentence or an internal abbreviation.

slides.title: Language models
slides.summary: Symbolic models provide a binary assessment of sentence well-formedness, whereas probabilistic language models estimate the likelihood of strings being valid, requiring all sentence probabilities to sum to one. While simple statistical approaches struggle with long-distance dependencies and lack meaning representation, more evolved neural models address these limitations by incorporating semantic information. Unlike interpretable symbolic rules, these complex models rely on parameter combinations that are difficult to tune individually but improve significantly with increased data volume.

slides.title: Uses of language models
slides.summary: Language models improve speech recognition, OCR, handwriting recognition, machine translation, text generation, and context-sensitive spelling correction by selecting the most probable sentences. For instance, they distinguish "I ate a tomato" from phonetically similar but unlikely alternatives like "eye eight atom eight oh". Similarly, they identify correct readings or translations based on sentence likelihood and fix errors such as changing "Their is a problem wit this sentence" to its more probable form.

slides.title: Completion prediction
slides.summary: Completion prediction refers to a language model's ability to predict the next word in a sentence, as illustrated by examples like "Please turn off your mobile ____" and "If he loses, he has only himself to ____". This concept underpins predictive text input systems, which guess what a user is typing and provide choices to complete the text.

slides.title: Statistical language model
slides.summary: A statistical language model computes sentence probabilities by counting occurrences in a large corpus, though exact sentence matching is often impractical due to data sparsity. Instead, the model estimates conditional probabilities based on limited preceding word contexts to determine the likelihood of the next word. This simple counting approach effectively calculates the global probability of word sequences for applications like text generation and assessing sentence well-formedness.

slides.title: Statistical language model
slides.summary: A statistical language model computes sentence probability by dividing the count of a specific sentence's occurrences in a corpus by the total number of sentences. For example, the probability of "the dog was running across the green field" is calculated as its frequency divided by 10^14, resulting in zero because the exact sentence does not appear in the data.

slides.title: Statistical language model
slides.summary: A statistical language model computes the joint probability of a word sequence by decomposing it into a product of conditional probabilities. For the sentence "the dog was running across the green field," this involves multiplying terms such as p(the), p(dog|the), and subsequent words conditioned on all preceding context. This decomposition transforms the complex joint probability calculation into a series of manageable conditional probability estimations.

slides.title: Statistical language model
slides.summary: Statistical language models compute the joint probability of a word sequence by decomposing it into a product of conditional probabilities. For the sentence "the dog was running across the green field," this involves multiplying terms like p(the) and p(dog|the), where each subsequent word depends on the preceding context. The model simplifies this computation by utilizing only a limited context rather than the entire history.

slides.title: Statistical language model
slides.summary: Statistical language models compute the joint probability of a word sequence by decomposing it into a product of conditional probabilities. For the sentence "the dog was running across the green field," this involves multiplying terms like p(the) and p(dog|the), where each subsequent word depends on preceding ones. This approach relies on using only a limited context to estimate these probabilities efficiently.

slides.title: Estimating probabilities
slides.summary: This slide presents formulas for estimating probabilities using word counts. The probability of a single word is the count of that word divided by the total token count, while conditional probabilities are calculated by dividing the count of a specific n-gram by the count of its preceding context. Examples include calculating p(dog|the) and p(green|across the) based on these frequency ratios.

slides.title: N-gram models
slides.summary: N-gram models estimate the probability of a word given its prior context, where multiplying individual probabilities yields the total sentence probability. These models rely on the Markov assumption, predicting future states based only on a limited history of $n-1$ words rather than the entire sequence. While this simplification ignores broader context and may reduce accuracy in some cases, it remains a practical approach for language modeling.

slides.title: Smoothing
slides.summary: Smoothing addresses data sparsity in probability estimation by preventing individual probabilities from becoming zero, which would otherwise nullify the entire sequence likelihood due to multiplication. Similar to Naive Bayes, techniques like add-one smoothing reassign probability mass to unseen events to ensure non-zero values. More advanced schemes such as Good-Turing, Back-off, and Kneser-Ney also exist to handle these estimation challenges effectively.

slides.title: Evaluation
slides.summary: Language models are evaluated by training on one corpus portion and testing on held-out text, where good models assign high probabilities to unseen sentences. The standard metric, perplexity, represents the average number of words a model hesitates between at each position; lower values indicate better performance as they reflect higher certainty in word prediction. This approach constitutes intrinsic evaluation, which assesses the model's standalone ability to predict language rather than its extrinsic utility in applications like speech recognition or machine translation.

slides.title: Inconveniences
slides.summary: The approach discussed is simple and effective for application to large text corpora. However, it remains an insufficient model of language due to its inability to handle long-distance dependencies and its lack of meaning representation. These limitations highlight the gap between statistical simplicity and true linguistic understanding.

slides.title: Long-distance dependencies
slides.summary: Limited context models like n-grams fail to predict long-distance dependencies because the correct word depends on distant sentence elements rather than immediate predecessors. Syntactic examples show verb agreement relies on the initial subject noun ("man" vs. "men"), while semantic examples demonstrate that verb choice ("flies" vs. "talks") depends on the head noun's meaning. Consequently, more complex language models are required to capture these relationships spanning the entire sentence structure.

slides.title: Lack of meaning
slides.summary: While discrete approaches in natural language processing work surprisingly well, they provide a poor representation of word meaning by treating words as atomic units. Although numerical probabilities for similar words like "apple" and "pear" are closer than those for unrelated words like "car," this method lacks an inherent understanding of semantic similarity. Consequently, word embeddings are introduced as a superior representation that allows networks to grasp how similar one word is to another without manual value assignment.

slides.title: Lack of meaning
slides.summary: Although the discrete approach in natural language processing works surprisingly well, it provides a poor representation of word meaning by treating words as atomic units. Models like Naive Bayes calculate probabilities independently, failing to capture semantic similarities; for instance, knowing "fantastic" implies positivity does not help predict that the similar word "sensational" also indicates positivity. Consequently, these basic statistical models ignore the logical connections between semantically related terms.

slides.title: Lack of meaning
slides.summary: The discrete approach is frequently used in natural language processing and performs surprisingly well, yet it remains a poor representation of word meaning. This method relies on atomic word representations where words are treated as isolated units without capturing semantic relationships, as illustrated by the binary vector examples for terms like "apple," "pear," "fantastic," and "sensational."

slides.title: Lack of meaning
slides.summary: The discrete approach is frequently used in natural language processing and performs surprisingly well, yet it offers a very poor representation of word meaning. This method relies on atomic word representations where each word is treated as an independent unit, illustrated by probability vectors for terms like "apple" or "fantastic". Consequently, this representation fails to capture semantic relationships between words, such as the similarity between "apple" and "pear."

slides.title: Introduction
slides.summary: Instead of discrete word representations, this slide introduces rich feature structures where words like "apple," "pear," and "car" are defined by properties such as being abstract, artifacts, or edible. This approach captures semantic similarity, as "apple" and "pear" share more features than either does with "car". However, because manually creating these structures is labor-intensive, the goal is to automatically extract these feature vectors from text rather than encoding them by hand.

slides.title: Distributional similarity
slides.summary: Distributional similarity relies on the distributional hypothesis, which posits that a word's meaning can be inferred from its surrounding contexts. This approach models words as vectors within a matrix based on co-occurrence counts with context words, allowing mathematical measures to compute semantic similarity between them. Unlike bigram models focused on prediction, this method identifies which words are semantically similar by analyzing how frequently they appear in comparable environments.

slides.title: Distributional similarity
slides.summary: Distributional similarity relies on the distributional hypothesis, which posits that a word's meaning can be inferred from its context. For instance, encountering an unknown term like "sooluceps" alongside descriptors such as "tasty," "sweet," and "freshly baked" allows one to deduce it refers to food. Consequently, semantic similarity is established by analyzing the surrounding words that define a term's usage.

slides.title: Distributional similarity
slides.summary: Distributional similarity relies on the distributional hypothesis, which posits that a word's meaning can be inferred by examining its context. The slide illustrates this using the word "sooluceps" paired with various descriptors like "tasty," "sweet," "stale," and "freshly baked". By analyzing these surrounding contexts, one can determine the semantic properties of the target word without explicit definitions.

slides.title: Matrix
slides.summary: A matrix captures the co-occurrence frequencies of two entities, as illustrated by a table pairing items like "raspberry" and "car" with attributes such as "red," "tasty," "fast," and "second-hand". The numerical values within the grid represent how often specific entity pairs appear together, providing a structured representation of these relationships for computational analysis.

slides.title: Matrix
slides.summary: A matrix captures the co-occurrence frequencies of two entities, as demonstrated by a table cross-referencing items like "raspberry," "strawberry," "car," and "truck" against attributes such as "red," "tasty," "fast," and "second-hand". The numerical values within the grid represent how often each specific pair appears together, with non-zero entries indicating observed associations while zeros denote the absence of co-occurrence.

slides.title: Matrix
slides.summary: A matrix captures the co-occurrence frequencies of two entities within a corpus, such as how often specific nouns appear with particular adjectives. For instance, "raspberry" and "strawberry" frequently co-occur with "red" and "tasty," while "car" and "truck" associate with "fast" and "second-hand" but not with "tasty". This structure quantifies these relationships by recording exact counts or zeros for each entity pair.

The numerical values within the matrix quantify how often each specific entity-attribute pair appears together, providing a structured representation of these relationships for computational analysis.

slides.title: Neural network: basics
slides.summary: A single neuron in a neural network functions identically to logistic regression, serving as the fundamental building block for these models. Like logistic regression, each neuron calculates the probability of an instance belonging to a specific class by weighting its input features with model parameters. This computation is mathematically expressed through matrix algebra, where inputs are multiplied by weight matrices and combined with bias factors to generate predictions.

slides.title: Logistic regression
slides.summary: Logistic regression is applied to spam classification by using word frequencies as features, where each feature $f_i$ is assigned a specific weight $w_i$. Words like "pharmacy" and "viagra" receive positive weights (0.4 and 1.2), indicating spam likelihood, while words such as "request" and "sending" have negative weights (-0.8 and -1.7). A bias term of 0.1 is also included in the model to adjust the classification threshold.

slides.title: Logistic regression
slides.summary: Logistic regression is applied to spam classification by using word frequencies as features, where each word has an associated weight. For the email "Pharmacy online: viagra best offer!", the score is calculated by summing the weights of present words (pharmacy, viagra, best, offer) and the bias, while absent words contribute zero. This results in a final score of 2.1 for the given example.

slides.title: Logistic regression
slides.summary: Binary logistic regression classifies emails as spam by calculating a linear score from word frequencies multiplied by specific weights, plus a bias term representing the prior probability of spam. This raw score, which ranges from negative to positive infinity, is transformed via the logistic function into a probability between 0 and 1. For instance, an email containing "pharmacy" and "viagra" yields a high spam probability (0.89), while one with "request" and "sending" results in a low probability (0.12).

slides.title: Logistic regression
slides.summary: Logistic regression addresses the difficulty of interpreting linear scores, which range from negative to positive infinity, by transforming them into probabilities using a non-linear logistic function. This transformation applies the formula $1 / (1 + e^{-x})$ to map scores onto a 0–1 scale. For instance, a score of -2.1 yields a probability of 0.89, while a score of 2.0 results in a probability of 0.12.

slides.title: Neuron = logistic regression
slides.summary: A single neuron performs the exact computation of logistic regression: inputs are multiplied by weights, summed with a bias term, and passed through a non-linear activation function (the logistic function) to map values from negative infinity to positive infinity into the range of zero to one. In a neural network, multiple neurons in a layer apply this same computation with different weights to an input vector, generating an output vector that serves as the input for subsequent layers. slides.title: Feed-forward
slides.summary: This slide defines a feed-forward multi-layer perceptron with two hidden layers, where an input vector of size 3 is transformed into an output vector of size 2 via intermediate hidden vectors of size 4. The architecture computes representations sequentially: the first layer applies weights (3×4) and bias to generate h1, which serves as input for the second layer using a 4×4 weight matrix to produce h2. Finally, a 4×2 weight matrix transforms h2 into the output y, completing the basic neural network structure.

slides.title: Feed-forward
slides.summary: The lecture defines a feed-forward multi-layer perceptron with two hidden layers, where the output $y$ is computed through sequential transformations: $h_1 = g(xW_1 + b_1)$ and $h_2 = g(h_1W_2 + b_2)$, followed by $y = h_2W_3$. The architecture utilizes weight matrices $W_1, W_2, W_3$ of sizes [3×4], [4×4], and [4×2] respectively, along with bias vectors $b_1, b_2$ of size 4. The function $g(\cdot)$ represents an elementwise non-linear activation applied at each hidden layer.

slides.title: Feed-forward
slides.summary: The lecture defines a feed-forward architecture as a multi-layer perceptron with two hidden layers, mathematically expressed through sequential transformations involving weights (W), biases (b), and an activation function (g). The network parameters, denoted as θ, include W1, W2, W3, b1, and b2. The slide explicitly identifies the use of multiple hidden layers as the defining characteristic of deep learning.

slides.title: Training
slides.summary: Training aims to predict correct labels by minimizing a loss function, $L(\hat{y}, y)$, which quantifies the mismatch between predicted output $\hat{y}$ and true output $y$. To achieve this, parameters $\theta$ are adjusted by computing the gradient of the loss function with respect to those parameters. This mathematical process guides the model in the direction that reduces the cost incurred from incorrect predictions, ultimately ensuring accurate label prediction on the training set.

slides.title: Training
slides.summary: Training utilizes the categorical cross-entropy loss function to quantify the difference between the true class distribution and the predicted distribution generated by a softmax output. While detailed mathematical derivations are outside this course's scope, the core objective is to optimize network parameters stochastically based on this quantified error against gold standard data.

slides.title: Training
slides.summary: Stochastic gradient descent minimizes total loss by computing gradients over small batches rather than the entire training set, avoiding computationally heavy full-corpus calculations. This approach updates parameters incrementally based on sampled examples instead of waiting for a complete pass. The learning rate hyperparameter controls step size, requiring a balance between large steps for speed and small steps to prevent overshooting the optimal destination.

slides.title: Training
slides.summary: Training utilizes stochastic gradient descent, where mini-batch size balances estimation quality against convergence speed. The backpropagation algorithm efficiently calculates gradients for parameters like weights and embeddings by propagating error through a computational graph to minimize prediction mismatch. While understanding these mathematical computations is essential, practitioners rely on existing automatic tools rather than performing manual derivations.

slides.title: Word embeddings
slides.summary: Word embeddings represent each word as a small, dense vector in a real-valued, low-dimensional space, typically with dimensions between 50 and 1000. These vectors form a matrix of size vocabulary by embedding dimension, where similar words possess similar vector representations. Unlike interpretable co-occurrence counts, the individual dimensions of these embeddings are not readily interpretable, yet they effectively capture semantic relationships that allow for computing word similarity.

slides.title: Word embeddings
slides.summary: Word embeddings represent each word as a small, dense vector in a low-dimensional real-valued space, typically with dimensions between 50 and 1000. Unlike traditional statistical models where words like "apple" and "pear" are represented by perpendicular vectors with no similarity, embeddings ensure that semantically similar words have closer vector representations. This approach allows the model to capture meaning by positioning related words nearer to each other compared to unrelated terms like "car."

slides.title: Word embeddings
slides.summary: Word embeddings represent each word $i$ as a small, dense vector $v_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$, where the dimension $d$ typically ranges from 50 to 1000. These vectors form a matrix of size $V \times d$, embedding words into a real-valued, low-dimensional space. A key property is that semantically similar words possess similar vector embeddings within this space.

slides.title: Neural word embeddings
slides.summary: Neural word embeddings represent each word as a dense vector of parameters (e.g., 50–300 values) rather than a single discrete value, forming an embedding matrix for the entire vocabulary. These vectors are automatically learned by training a neural network to predict the next word in a sequence based on preceding context words. By optimizing these embeddings to minimize prediction error, the network captures semantic similarities between words, enabling richer meaning representations useful for downstream tasks like sentiment analysis.

slides.title: Embeddings through language modeling
slides.summary: This slide introduces generating embeddings by training a neural network on the language modeling task: predicting the next word in a sequence based on the previous one. The architecture consists of one non-linear hidden layer and a softmax classification layer, with parameters initialized randomly and optimized to maximize the probability of the correct word. This approach allows the network to learn meaningful vector representations autonomously rather than relying on discrete word counts or pre-existing values.

slides.title: Embeddings through language modeling
slides.summary: Embeddings through language modeling involve predicting the next word in a sequence based on the previous word. This approach utilizes a neural network architecture consisting of one non-linear hidden layer and one softmax layer for classification. The model parameters are selected to optimize the probability of correctly predicting the target word.

slides.title: Embeddings through error detection
slides.summary: Embeddings through error detection involve taking a correct sentence and creating a corrupted counterpart by randomly altering words, such as changing "white" to "heavy". The network is trained to assign a higher score to the correct version and a lower score to the corrupted one. This optimization process allows the model to learn an embedding matrix that captures semantic similarity between words.

slides.title: Embeddings through error detection
slides.summary: Embeddings through error detection involve taking a correct sentence and generating a corrupted counterpart. The network is then trained to assign a higher score to the correct version of each sentence compared to its corrupted version, thereby learning meaningful representations through this discrimination task.

slides.title: Word2vec
slides.summary: Word2vec is a popular, lightweight neural network approach for generating word embeddings that uses fewer parameters and no hidden layers compared to heavier models. It relies on a softmax classifier and implements two distinct architectures: Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW), which predicts the current word from surrounding context, and Skip-gram, which predicts surrounding words based on the current context word.

slides.title: CBOW
slides.summary: In the Continuous Bag-of-Words (CBOW) model, the current word $w_t$ is predicted based on its surrounding context words. This prediction is generated by calculating the sum of the embeddings associated with those context words.

slides.title: Skip-gram
slides.summary: The Skip-gram model reverses the previous approach by taking a target word as input to predict its surrounding context words, such as predicting context for "wine". Unlike models with hidden layers, this architecture lacks one, making parameter estimation easier and the approach more lightweight. Additionally, the parameters for each softmax classifier used in these predictions are shared across the model.

slides.title: Negative sampling
slides.summary: Negative sampling addresses the high computational cost of full softmax classifiers by calculating scores only for the correct context and a selected number of incorrect contexts. The objective is to maximize the score for the correct context while simultaneously minimizing the scores for the wrong ones, thereby reducing the overall computation required during training.

slides.title: Word similarity
slides.summary: Word similarity is determined by computing the angle and cosine between word vectors to identify the most similar neighbors for a target word. For instance, 'Belgium' retrieves countries like 'Netherlands', while 'Jesus' yields related terms such as 'Christ' and 'Resurrection'. Similarly, color words like 'red' associate with 'yellow' and 'pink', and art forms like 'painting' link to 'sculpture' and 'watercolor', demonstrating how embeddings capture semantic relationships.

slides.title: Computing analogies
slides.summary: Computing analogies involve questions structured as "a is to b as c is to d," where a system receives three terms and must compute the fourth. Examples include syntactic analogies like "apple is to apples as car is to ?" and semantic ones such as "man is to woman as king is to ?". The objective is to determine if the system can successfully solve these analogy problems based on the provided inputs.

slides.title: Computing analogies
slides.summary: Computing analogies relies on the principle that relational directions remain consistent within a high-dimensional vector space, expressed as $a - b \approx c - d$. To solve for an unknown term like "queen" in "man is to woman as king is to ?", one calculates the vector $c - a + b$ and identifies the vocabulary word with the highest cosine similarity to this result. This process involves iterating through all embeddings to find the vector that best matches the computed directional relationship.

slides.title: Computing analogies
slides.summary: The lecture demonstrates that embedding matrices automatically capture relational information, enabling networks to solve analogies like "France is to Paris as Italy is to Rome" by identifying consistent vector directions. While the model successfully handles country-capital pairs and comparative adjectives, it does not always produce optimal results, such as associating France with tapas instead of sushi. These examples from Mikolov et al. (2013) illustrate that rich 300-dimensional spaces encode semantic relationships, though this raises broader questions regarding network interpretability.

slides.title: Prediction-based vs. count-based
slides.summary: Count-based methods extract co-occurrence frequencies from a corpus to create explicit matrices, while prediction-based approaches induce parameters by predicting the correct word to generate embeddings. Although initially viewed as distinct with prediction-based methods performing better, emerging evidence proves they are equivalent because both fundamentally rely on co-occurrence data. Applying dimensionality reduction to count-based matrices yields results similar to those from prediction-based embedding approaches.

slides.title: Word embeddings in practice
slides.summary: Word embeddings are frequently used for pretraining because they are unsupervised, requiring only plain text to leverage large datasets with fast algorithms. This approach allows models to start from an informed position by initializing them with pretrained embeddings before fine-tuning for specific tasks.
